reminder: The divergence of a vector field measures how fast the field spreads out volume at each point.
definition: On a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ of dimension $n$ with a [volume form](c:volume-form) $\omega$, the divergence of a [vector field](c:vector-field) $X$ is the unique [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $\operatorname{div}_\omega X$ with $\mathcal L_X\omega=(\operatorname{div}_\omega X)\,\omega$, where $\mathcal L_X$ is the [Lie derivative](c:lie-derivative). On $\mathbb R^n$ with $\omega=dx^1\wedge\dots\wedge dx^n$ this gives $\operatorname{div}X=\sum_i\partial X^i/\partial x^i$.
examples: On $\mathbb R^3$ with the standard volume form, the field $X=(x,y,z)$ has $\operatorname{div}X=3$; its flow expands volume.
The rotation field $X=(-y,x)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ has divergence $0$, and its flow keeps area.
Non-example: a vector field on a manifold with no chosen volume form has no divergence, because $\operatorname{div}_\omega X$ depends on $\omega$.
Non-example: the [curl](c:curl) of a field on $\mathbb R^3$ is again a vector field, so it is not a divergence, which is a function.

reminder: A divisor is a formal integer sum of subvarieties of codimension one.
definition: On a normal [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $X$, a divisor is a finite formal sum $\sum n_iD_i$ with $n_i\in\mathbb Z$, where each $D_i$ is an irreducible closed subvariety of [codimension](c:codimension) one. A nonzero [rational function](c:rational-function) $f$ gives the divisor $\operatorname{div}(f)=\sum\operatorname{ord}_{D}(f)\,D$, which counts zeros of $f$ with positive sign and poles with negative sign.
examples: On a curve, a divisor is a finite integer combination of points, such as $2P-3Q$.
On the projective line, the function $f=x$ has divisor $P_0-P_\infty$: a simple zero at $0$ and a simple pole at $\infty$.
On a surface, an irreducible curve $C$ gives the divisor $C$, and a sum such as $3C_1-C_2$ is a divisor.
Non-example: a point on a surface has codimension two, so it is not a prime divisor there.

reminder: The factorial $n!$ is the product of all natural numbers from $1$ to $n$.
definition: For a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$, the factorial is the [product](c:product) $n!=1\cdot2\cdots n$, with $0!=1$ for the empty product. It satisfies $(n+1)!=(n+1)\,n!$ and counts the [permutations](c:permutation) of an $n$-element set.
examples: $5!=1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5=120$.
Three books on a shelf have $3!=6$ possible orders.
$0!=1$, because the empty product is $1$; this makes $\binom{n}{n}=\frac{n!}{n!\,0!}=1$ correct.
Non-example: $(-1)!$ is undefined, because the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function) has a pole at $0$.

steps: Define $\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ for $\operatorname{Re}z>0$.
Integrate by parts to get $\Gamma(z+1)=z\,\Gamma(z)$.
Since $\Gamma(1)=1$, induction gives $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$ for every natural number $n$.
links.why: The Gamma function extends $n!$ to complex arguments, so formulas with factorials continue to non-integers.

reminder: The Gaussian curvature of a surface at a point is the product of its two principal curvatures there.
definition: At a point of a [surface](c:surface) in $\mathbb R^3$, the Gaussian curvature is $K=k_1k_2$, where $k_1$ and $k_2$ are the two [principal curvatures](c:principal-curvature), the extreme values of the normal [curvature](c:curvature). By Gauss's Theorema Egregium, $K$ depends only on the intrinsic metric of the surface.
examples: A sphere of radius $r$ has $K=1/r^2$ at every point.
A plane has $K=0$, and so has a cylinder, because one principal curvature of the cylinder is $0$.
A saddle point has principal curvatures of opposite sign, so $K<0$.
Non-example: the mean curvature $H=(k_1+k_2)/2$ is not intrinsic; a plane has $H=0$ and a cylinder of radius $r$ has $H=1/(2r)$, though both have $K=0$.

steps: Take a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $M$ of dimension $2$, such as a surface with its induced metric.
At each point $p$, the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) $T_pM$ is the only $2$-plane in $T_pM$.
So the sectional curvature of $M$ at $p$ is one number, and it equals the Gaussian curvature $K(p)$.
links.why: It shows that the sectional curvature of higher dimensions reduces to the Gaussian curvature of surfaces.

reminder: A group is a set with an associative operation that has an identity and gives every element an inverse.
definition: A group is a [set](c:set) $G$ with a [binary operation](c:binary-operation) $\cdot$ that is [associative](c:associative-operation), has an [identity element](c:identity-element) $e$ with $e\cdot g=g\cdot e=g$ for all $g$, and gives each $g$ an inverse $g^{-1}$ with $g\cdot g^{-1}=g^{-1}\cdot g=e$.
examples: The integers with addition form a group: the identity is $0$ and the inverse of $n$ is $-n$.
The rotations and reflections of a square form a group of order $8$ that is not commutative.
The nonzero real numbers with multiplication form a group, with $x^{-1}=1/x$.
Non-example: the natural numbers with addition have an identity but no inverses, because no $n$ gives $1+n=0$.

steps: Take a group $G$ and keep only its operation and its identity element.
These satisfy associativity and the identity law, so $G$ is a monoid.
The added condition for a group is that every element has an inverse.
links.why: Facts about monoids, such as the uniqueness of the identity, hold in every group.

steps: Take an abelian group $A$, with an associative operation, an identity and inverses.
Then $A$ is a group that also satisfies $ab=ba$ for all $a,b$.
So a group is abelian exactly when this extra commutation law holds.
links.why: Every theorem about groups applies to abelian groups, and commutativity is the one extra condition.

steps: Take a Lie group $G$, a group that is also a smooth manifold.
Its multiplication and its inversion are smooth maps.
Forget the smooth structure; what remains is an ordinary group.
links.why: It shows that Lie groups inherit all of group theory and add smoothness.

reminder: Scaling every argument of a homogeneous function of degree $k$ by $\lambda$ scales its value by $\lambda^k$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [ring](c:ring) and let $f$ be a [function](c:function) of $n$ arguments in $R$-[modules](c:module) with values in an $R$-module. The function $f$ is homogeneous of degree $k$ if $f(\lambda x_1,\dots,\lambda x_n)=\lambda^kf(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ for all $\lambda\in R$. For real functions one also allows real $k$ and only $\lambda>0$.
examples: The function $f(x,y)=x^2+xy$ has degree $2$, because $f(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda^2f(x,y)$.
Every linear map is homogeneous of degree $1$.
The norm $f(x)=|x|$ on $\mathbb R$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ for $\lambda>0$ only, since $|-x|\ne-|x|$.
Non-example: $f(x)=x+1$ is not homogeneous, because $f(0)=1$ forces degree $0$, but $f(2)=3\neq f(1)=2$.

steps: Take a polynomial $p$ whose monomials all have the same total degree $d$.
Each monomial $x^\alpha$ satisfies $(\lambda x)^\alpha=\lambda^dx^\alpha$.
Adding the monomials gives $p(\lambda x)=\lambda^dp(x)$, so $p$ is homogeneous of degree $d$.
links.why: Homogeneous polynomials are the polynomial case, so facts about homogeneous functions apply to them.

steps: Take a linear map $T$ between modules over $R$.
It satisfies $T(\lambda x)=\lambda T(x)$ for all $\lambda\in R$.
So $T$ is homogeneous of degree $1$; linearity adds the condition $T(x+y)=T(x)+T(y)$.
links.why: It shows that linear maps are the additive functions among those of degree one.

reminder: A hyperplane is a linear or affine subspace of codimension one.
definition: In a finite-dimensional [affine space](c:affine-space) of dimension $n$, a hyperplane is an [affine subspace](c:affine-subspace) of dimension $n-1$, that is of [codimension](c:codimension) one; in a vector space, a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) of that dimension. Equivalently, it is a set $\{x:\varphi(x)=c\}$ for a nonzero linear functional $\varphi$ and a constant $c$.
examples: A line in the plane $\mathbb R^2$ is a hyperplane.
The plane $x+y+z=1$ in $\mathbb R^3$ is an affine hyperplane, and $x+y+z=0$ is a linear hyperplane through the origin.
The set $\{x_n=0\}$ in $\mathbb R^n$ is the coordinate hyperplane that separates the two half-spaces $x_n>0$ and $x_n<0$.
Non-example: a line in $\mathbb R^3$ has codimension two, so it is not a hyperplane.

steps: Take an affine hyperplane $H=\{x:\varphi(x)=c\}$ and pick a point $p\in H$.
Then $H=p+\ker\varphi$, and $\ker\varphi$ is a linear subspace.
So $H$ is an affine subspace, and the added condition is codimension one.
links.why: It shows that every theorem about affine subspaces applies to hyperplanes.

reminder: The Jacobian matrix of a map holds all first-order partial derivatives of its component functions.
definition: For a [differentiable map](c:differentiable-map) $f=(f_1,\dots,f_m)\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, the Jacobian matrix at $x$ is the $m\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) whose entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) $\partial f_i/\partial x_j$ at $x$. It represents the [total derivative](c:total-derivative) of $f$ at $x$, the best linear approximation of $f$ near $x$.
examples: The polar map $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ has Jacobian determinant $r$.
A linear map $x\mapsto Ax$ has the Jacobian matrix $A$ at every point.
For $f(x,y)=(x^2y,\,x+y)$ the first row is $(2xy,\;x^2)$ and the second row is $(1,\;1)$.
Non-example: for $f(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2)$ with $f(0,0)=0$, both partials exist at $0$, but $f$ is not differentiable there, so the row $(0\ 0)$ does not describe $f$ near $0$.

steps: Take a differentiable function $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, so $n=m=1$.
Its Jacobian matrix at $x$ has one row and one column.
The single entry is the ordinary derivative $f'(x)$.
links.why: It shows that the Jacobian matrix is the derivative of a function of one variable, written for many variables.

steps: Take a differentiable scalar function $f\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, so $m=1$.
Its Jacobian matrix at $x$ has one row, with entries $\partial f/\partial x_j$.
That row is the [gradient](c:gradient) of $f$ written as a row vector.
links.why: It shows that the gradient is the Jacobian matrix of a scalar function.

reminder: A linear subspace is a subset of a vector space that contains $0$ and is closed under addition and scaling.
definition: A linear subspace of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a [field](c:field) $F$ is a [subset](c:subset) $W\subseteq V$ with $0\in W$ such that $u+v\in W$ and $\lambda u\in W$ for all $u,v\in W$ and $\lambda\in F$. With the restricted operations, $W$ is itself a vector space.
examples: In $\mathbb R^3$, the plane $\{(x,y,z):x+y+z=0\}$ is a linear subspace.
The kernel of a [linear map](c:linear-map) is a linear subspace of its domain.
The polynomials of degree at most $3$ form a linear subspace of the space of all polynomials.
Non-example: the plane $x+y+z=1$ misses $0$ and is not closed under addition.

steps: Take a linear subspace $W$ of $V$ and translate it by the vector $0$.
The translate $0+W=W$ is an affine subspace of $V$.
An affine subspace is linear exactly when it contains $0$, which is the added condition.
links.why: It shows that linear subspaces are the affine subspaces through the origin.

steps: Take a closed subspace $W$ of a topological vector space $V$.
Ignore the topology; $W$ is still closed under addition and scaling.
So $W$ is a linear subspace, and closedness in $V$ is the added condition.
links.why: It shows that a closed subspace is a linear subspace with an extra topological condition.

reminder: The localization $S^{-1}R$ is the ring of fractions $r/s$ in which every element of $S$ has an inverse.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $S\subseteq R$ a [multiplicative subset](c:multiplicative-subset). The localization $S^{-1}R$ is the set of [equivalence classes](c:equivalence-class) $r/s$ of pairs $(r,s)$ with $s\in S$, where $r/s=r'/s'$ when $t(rs'-r's)=0$ for some $t\in S$, with the usual rules for sums and products of fractions. The map $r\mapsto r/1$ is a ring homomorphism that makes every element of $S$ invertible, and it is universal for this property.
examples: Inverting the powers of $2$ in $\mathbb Z$ gives the ring $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ of dyadic fractions.
For an integral domain $R$ and $S=R\setminus\{0\}$, the localization is the [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions), such as $\mathbb Q$ for $\mathbb Z$.
Inverting a single element $f$ of $R$ gives $R[1/f]$, the ring of functions defined where $f\neq0$.
Non-example: the quotient $\mathbb Z/n$ with $n\ge2$ is not a localization of $\mathbb Z$, because it forces $n=0$ instead of making elements invertible.

steps: Take an integral domain $R$ and let $S=R\setminus\{0\}$.
The set $S$ is multiplicative, because a product of nonzero elements is nonzero.
Then $S^{-1}R$ has an inverse for every nonzero element, so it is the field of fractions of $R$.
links.why: It shows that the field of fractions is the largest localization of a domain.

reminder: A sequence of functions converges locally uniformly when every point has a neighbourhood where the convergence is uniform.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space), $Y$ a [metric space](c:metric-space) and $f_n,f\colon X\to Y$ functions. The sequence $(f_n)$ converges locally uniformly to $f$ if every point of $X$ has a neighbourhood on which $f_n\to f$ [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence). When $X$ is locally compact, for example an open set of $\mathbb C$, this means uniform convergence on every [compact subspace](c:compact-subspace).
examples: The functions $f_n(x)=x^n$ converge to $0$ locally uniformly on $(-1,1)$, but not uniformly on $(-1,1)$.
The partial sums of a power series converge locally uniformly on its open disc of convergence.
If holomorphic functions $f_n$ converge locally uniformly, the limit is holomorphic, which is the setting of Hurwitz's theorem.
Non-example: $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$ converges pointwise to a discontinuous function, so the convergence is not locally uniform near $1$.

steps: Suppose $f_n\to f$ uniformly on all of $X$.
Then every point of $X$ has the neighbourhood $X$ itself, on which the convergence is uniform.
So uniform convergence is locally uniform; the converse fails for $x^n$ on $(-1,1)$.
links.why: It shows that local uniform convergence is the weaker notion that most theorems of analysis really need.

steps: Suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly and fix a point $x$.
Choose a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ on which $f_n\to f$ uniformly.
Uniform convergence on $U$ gives $f_n(x)\to f(x)$, so the convergence is pointwise; uniformity on neighbourhoods is the added condition.
links.why: It shows what local uniform convergence adds to pointwise convergence.

reminder: A maximal element of a poset has no strictly greater element in the poset.
definition: In a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) $(P,\le)$, an element $m$ is maximal if no $x\in P$ satisfies $m<x$, that is, $m\le x$ implies $x=m$. Unlike a greatest element, a maximal element need not be an [upper bound](c:upper-bound) of all of $P$.
examples: In $\{1,2,3,4,6\}$ ordered by divisibility, the elements $4$ and $6$ are maximal, but neither is greatest.
In the subsets of a set ordered by inclusion, the whole set is the only maximal element.
The proper ideals of a ring, ordered by inclusion, have the maximal ideals as their maximal elements.
Non-example: in $\mathbb N$ with the usual order no element is maximal, because $n<n+1$ for every $n$.

steps: Take a ring $R$ and the set $P$ of proper ideals of $R$, ordered by inclusion.
A maximal ideal is a proper ideal $M$ that no other proper ideal strictly contains.
That is exactly a maximal element of $P$.
links.why: It shows that a maximal ideal is the maximal-element notion applied to a chosen poset.

steps: Take a group $G$ and the set $P$ of proper subgroups of $G$, ordered by inclusion.
A maximal subgroup is a proper subgroup that no other proper subgroup strictly contains.
That is exactly a maximal element of $P$.
links.why: It shows that maximal subgroups are maximal elements of the poset of proper subgroups.

reminder: The minimal polynomial of an element is the monic polynomial of least degree that has the element as a root.
definition: Let $L/K$ be a [field extension](c:field-extension) and $a\in L$ an [algebraic element](c:algebraic-element) over $K$. Its minimal polynomial is the unique [monic polynomial](c:monic-polynomial) $m\in K[x]$ of least degree with $m(a)=0$; it is [irreducible](c:irreducible-polynomial) and divides every polynomial in $K[x]$ that vanishes at $a$. For a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A$ over $K$, it is the monic polynomial of least degree with $m(A)=0$.
examples: The number $\sqrt2$ has minimal polynomial $x^2-2$ over $\mathbb Q$.
The imaginary unit $i$ has minimal polynomial $x^2+1$ over $\mathbb R$, and $x-i$ over $\mathbb C$.
The identity matrix $I_n$ has minimal polynomial $x-1$, while its [characteristic polynomial](c:characteristic-polynomial) $(x-1)^n$ has degree $n$.
Non-example: $x^2-4$ is not the minimal polynomial of $2$ over $\mathbb Q$, because it is reducible and $x-2$ has lower degree.

reminder: A partial derivative differentiates a function of several variables in one variable while the others stay fixed.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of several real variables, the partial derivative with respect to $x_i$ at a point $a$ is the [derivative](c:derivative) at $t=a_i$ of the one-variable function $t\mapsto f(a_1,\dots,t,\dots,a_n)$. As a limit it is $\partial f/\partial x_i(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(f(a+he_i)-f(a)\bigr)/h$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th unit vector.
examples: For $f(x,y)=x^2y$ we have $\partial f/\partial x=2xy$ and $\partial f/\partial y=x^2$.
For $f(x,y)=\sin(xy)$ we have $\partial f/\partial x=y\cos(xy)$.
The partial derivatives of $f(x,y)=x+3y$ are the constants $1$ and $3$.
Non-example: $f(x,y)=|x|+|y|$ has no partial derivative in $x$ at $(0,0)$, because $t\mapsto|t|$ has no derivative at $0$.

steps: Take a function $f$ of one variable, so $n=1$ and $e_1=1$.
The only partial derivative is the limit $\lim_{h\to0}(f(a+h)-f(a))/h$.
That limit is the ordinary derivative $f'(a)$.
links.why: It shows that partial derivatives are ordinary derivatives taken along one coordinate.

steps: Take a function $f$ of $n$ variables and a direction $v\in\mathbb R^n$.
The directional derivative along $v$ is $\lim_{h\to0}(f(a+hv)-f(a))/h$.
Choosing $v=e_i$, the $i$th unit vector, gives the partial derivative $\partial f/\partial x_i$.
links.why: It shows that a partial derivative is a directional derivative along a coordinate axis.

reminder: A presheaf is a contravariant functor from a category to sets.
definition: A presheaf on a [category](c:category) $C$ is a [contravariant functor](c:contravariant-functor) $F$ from $C$ to sets, that is, a [functor](c:functor) from the [opposite category](c:opposite-category) $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ to sets. It gives a set $F(U)$ to each object $U$ and a restriction map $F(V)\to F(U)$ to each morphism $U\to V$, compatibly with identities and composition. On the open sets of a [topological space](c:topological-space), the restriction map restricts a section over $V$ to a smaller open set $U\subseteq V$.
examples: On a space $X$, give each open set $U$ the set of continuous real functions on $U$, with restriction of functions.
The constant presheaf gives every open set the same set $A$, with identity restriction maps.
For a group $G$ seen as a one-object category, a presheaf is a set with a right $G$-action.
Non-example: compactly supported functions $U\mapsto C_c(U)$ with extension by zero map $F(U)\to F(V)$ for $U\subseteq V$, so they form a covariant functor, not a presheaf.

steps: Take a sheaf $F$ on a topological space $X$.
Keep only the sets $F(U)$ and the restriction maps between them.
These form a presheaf, and the gluing condition for open covers is what a sheaf adds.
links.why: It shows that a sheaf is a presheaf with the gluing condition, so presheaf results apply to sheaves.

reminder: A product measure gives each measurable rectangle the product of the measures of its two sides.
definition:
For [measure spaces](c:measure-space) $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,
u)$, a product measure is a [measure](c:measure) $\mu	imes
u$ on the product [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) of the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $X	imes Y$ with $(\mu	imes
u)(A	imes B)=\mu(A)\,
u(B)$ for all measurable rectangles. When both measures are [sigma-finite](c:sigma-finite-measure), exactly one such measure exists.
examples: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$ is the product of Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ with itself.
The product of two probability measures is the joint law of two independent random variables.
The product of counting measure on $\{1,2\}$ and Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ gives each set $\{i\}\times B$ the measure of $B$.

Non-example: for Lebesgue measure and counting measure on $[0,1]$, counting measure is not sigma-finite, so the rectangle rule fixes no single product measure and the diagonal gives different iterated integrals.

reminder: The S-matrix gives the probability amplitude for each incoming particle state to scatter into each outgoing state.
definition: In quantum field theory, the S-matrix is the [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) $S$ on the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) of asymptotic particle states whose matrix elements $\langle\mathrm{out}|S|\mathrm{in}\rangle$ are the probability amplitudes for scattering from an initial state of free particles to a final one. Its squared moduli give the scattering probabilities, and in perturbation theory it is the time-ordered exponential of the interaction.
examples: With no interaction, $S$ is the identity operator: the outgoing state equals the incoming state.
In quantum electrodynamics, the lowest-order amplitude for electron-electron scattering comes from the Feynman diagram with one exchanged photon.
The squared modulus $|\langle\mathrm{out}|S|\mathrm{in}\rangle|^2$ of an element gives a transition probability, from which cross sections follow.
Non-example: the Hamiltonian $H$ generates time evolution over any interval and is not the S-matrix, which only compares asymptotic past states to asymptotic future states.

reminder: A set is a collection of distinct objects, and two sets with the same elements are equal.
definition: A set is a collection of distinct objects, called its [elements](c:element), and one writes $x\in S$ when $x$ is an element of $S$. By the [axiom of extensionality](c:axiom-of-extensionality), two sets with the same elements are equal, so a set is determined by which objects it contains.
examples: The sets $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{3,2,1,1\}$ are equal, because order and repeats do not matter.
The set of even integers is $\{n\in\mathbb Z: n=2k\text{ for some }k\in\mathbb Z\}$.
The [empty set](c:empty-set) $\varnothing$ has no elements, and $\{\varnothing\}$ has exactly one.
Non-example: the collection of all sets that are not members of themselves is not a set, by Russell's paradox.

steps: Take a finite set $S$, one that has exactly $n$ elements for a natural number $n$.
It is a set, so extensionality holds for it.
A set is finite when a bijection with $\{1,\dots,n\}$ exists, which is the added condition.
links.why: It shows that finite sets are the sets that can be counted, with no change to the basic notion.

reminder: The stabilizer of a point is the subgroup of group elements that fix the point.
definition: Let a [group](c:group) $G$ act on a set $X$ by a [group action](c:group-action). The stabilizer of $x\in X$ is $\mathrm{Stab}_G(x)=\{g\in G:g\cdot x=x\}$, which is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$. Its cosets correspond one to one with the points of the [orbit](c:orbit) of $x$.
examples: Let $S_3$ permute $\{1,2,3\}$; the stabilizer of $3$ is $\{e,(1\,2)\}$.
Let $SO(3)$ rotate $\mathbb R^3$; the stabilizer of a nonzero vector is the group of rotations about its axis.
If $G$ acts on itself by left multiplication, every stabilizer is the trivial subgroup.
Non-example: the set of $g$ with $g\cdot x=y$ for a point $y\neq x$ is not a subgroup, because it does not contain the identity.

reminder: An embedded submanifold is a subset of a manifold that looks like a coordinate subspace in suitable charts.
definition: A subset $S$ of a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is an embedded submanifold of dimension $k$ if it is the image of a smooth [embedding](c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds) of a $k$-dimensional manifold into $M$. Equivalently, around each point of $S$ there is a chart of $M$ in which $S$ becomes the coordinate subspace $\mathbb R^k\times\{0\}$.
examples: The unit sphere $S^n$ is a submanifold of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$.
The graph of a smooth function $f\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is a submanifold of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$.
The preimage of a [regular value](c:regular-value) of a smooth map is a submanifold of the domain.
Non-example: the cross $\{(x,y):xy=0\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ is not a submanifold, because near the origin it is not a coordinate line in any chart.

reminder: A family of integrable functions is uniformly integrable if the integrals over regions where the functions are large are uniformly small.
definition: On a finite [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mu)$, such as a probability space, a family $\mathcal F$ of [integrable functions](c:integrable-function) is uniformly integrable if $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\int_{\{|f|>K\}}|f|\,d\mu\to0$ as $K\to\infty$. Such a family has a bounded norm in the [L1 space](c:l1-space), since $\int|f|\,d\mu\le K\mu(X)+\sup_{f}\int_{\{|f|>K\}}|f|\,d\mu$.
examples: A single integrable function, or a finite family of integrable functions, is uniformly integrable.
A family bounded in $L^p$ for some $p>1$ on a probability space is uniformly integrable, because $\int_{\{|f|>K\}}|f|\le\|f\|_p^p/K^{p-1}$.
A family dominated by one integrable function $g$, that is $|f|\le g$ for all $f$, is uniformly integrable.
Non-example: $f_n=n\,\mathbf 1_{[0,1/n]}$ on $[0,1]$ has $\int f_n=1$, but $\int_{\{f_n>K\}}f_n=1$ for $n>K$, so the family is not uniformly integrable.

reminder: A unitary representation of a group acts on a Hilbert space by unitary operators.
definition: A unitary representation of a [group](c:group) $G$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $\pi\colon G\to U(H)$ into the group of [unitary operators](c:unitary-operator) of $H$. For a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$, one also asks that $g\mapsto\pi(g)v$ is continuous for every $v\in H$.
examples: The group $\mathbb R$ acts on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ by translations: $(\pi(t)f)(x)=f(x-t)$.
Every finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group is unitary for a suitable inner product, found by averaging over the group.
A locally compact group $G$ acts on $L^2(G)$, taken with Haar measure, by left translation of functions.
Non-example: the defining representation of $SL_2(\mathbb R)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ is not unitary for any inner product, because its matrices are unbounded but unitary operators have norm $1$.

steps: Take a unitary representation $\pi\colon G\to U(H)$.
Each $\pi(g)$ is an invertible linear operator on the vector space $H$, so $\pi$ is a representation of $G$.
Unitarity is the added condition: every $\pi(g)$ preserves the inner product of $H$.
links.why: It shows that general representation theory applies to unitary representations, which add an invariant inner product.

reminder: The weak-star topology is the coarsest topology on a dual space that makes every evaluation map continuous.
definition: Let $X$ be a [normed space](c:normed-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$. The weak-star topology on $X^*$ is the coarsest topology for which every [evaluation map](c:evaluation-map) $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(x)$, with $x\in X$, is continuous. Thus $\varphi_i\to\varphi$ in this topology exactly when $\varphi_i(x)\to\varphi(x)$ for every $x\in X$.
examples: On $\ell^\infty=(\ell^1)^*$, the unit vectors $e_n$ converge to $0$ weak-star, since $\sum_kx_ke_n(k)=x_n\to0$ for each $x\in\ell^1$.
By the Banach-Alaoglu theorem, the closed unit ball of $X^*$ is compact in the weak-star topology.
On the dual of $C[0,1]$, point evaluations $\delta_{x_n}$ converge weak-star to $\delta_x$ whenever $x_n\to x$.
Non-example: the unit vectors $e_n$ do not converge to $0$ in the norm topology of $\ell^\infty$, because $\|e_n\|=1$, so the norm topology is not the weak-star topology.

steps: View each functional $\varphi\in X^*$ as a function $X\to\mathbb K$.
The topology of pointwise convergence on such functions is the coarsest one that makes every evaluation at a point continuous.
Restrict it to the subset $X^*$ of continuous linear functionals; the result is the weak-star topology.
links.why: It shows that weak-star convergence is pointwise convergence on $X$, restricted to continuous linear functionals.

reminder: A chain complex is a sequence of abelian groups with boundary maps whose composite of two consecutive maps is zero.
definition: A chain complex is a sequence of [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) $C_n$ with [group homomorphisms](c:group-homomorphism) $\partial_n\colon C_n\to C_{n-1}$ such that $\partial_{n-1}\circ\partial_n=0$ for all $n$. Then the [image](c:image) of $\partial_{n+1}$ lies inside the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) of $\partial_n$, and the quotient of the second by the first is the homology group $H_n$.
examples: The simplicial chains of a triangle form $C_2=\mathbb Z\to C_1=\mathbb Z^3\to C_0=\mathbb Z^3$, where the boundary of the triangle is the sum of its three oriented edges, and the endpoints cancel in pairs.
The singular chain complex of a topological space has the boundary of a singular simplex as its differential.
Every [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) of abelian groups is a chain complex with all homology groups equal to $0$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{1}\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{1}\mathbb Z$ is a sequence of groups, but the composite is the identity and not zero, so it is not a chain complex.

steps: Take an exact sequence $\cdots\to C_{n+1}\to C_n\to C_{n-1}\to\cdots$.
Exactness at $C_n$ says that the image of $\partial_{n+1}$ equals the kernel of $\partial_n$.
So $\partial_n\circ\partial_{n+1}=0$, and the sequence is a chain complex with all homology equal to $0$.
links.why: It shows that an exact sequence is a chain complex with no homology.

reminder: The circle average of a function is its mean value over a circle of given center and radius.
definition: For a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f$ near a point $a\in\mathbb C$ and a radius $r>0$, the circle average of $f$ at $a$ with radius $r$ is $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(a+re^{i\theta})\,d\theta$. It is the mean value of $f$ over the [circle](c:circle) of radius $r$ around $a$, computed with an [integral](c:integral) over the angle.
examples: For a harmonic function $u$, the circle average at $a$ equals $u(a)$ for every radius; this is the [mean value property](c:mean-value-property).
For $f(z)=|z|^2$ at $a=0$, the circle average with radius $r$ is $r^2$.
For $f(z)=\log|z-b|$ at $a=0$ with $r\neq|b|$, the circle average is $\log\max(r,|b|)$, the identity behind Jensen's formula.
Non-example: the average of $f$ over the whole disc of radius $r$ is an area average, a different quantity, because it weights the interior points of the disc.

reminder: A colimit of a diagram is a cocone through which every other cocone factors in exactly one way.
definition: For a [diagram](c:diagram) $D\colon J\to C$ in a [category](c:category) $C$, a colimit is a [cocone](c:cocone) $(L,\ \iota_j\colon D(j)\to L)$ that is universal: for every cocone $(A,\ f_j)$ there is exactly one morphism $u\colon L\to A$ with $u\circ\iota_j=f_j$ for all $j$. By the [universal property](c:universal-property), a colimit is unique up to unique isomorphism.
examples: The disjoint union of two sets is the colimit of the diagram with two objects and no arrows.
The pushout of $B\leftarrow A\to C$ is the colimit of that span.
In abelian groups, the chain $\mathbb Z/2\to\mathbb Z/4\to\mathbb Z/8\to\cdots$ of inclusions has the colimit $\mathbb Z[1/2]/\mathbb Z$.
Non-example: $\{a,b,c\}$ with the inclusions of $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ is a cocone but not a colimit, because a map out of it can send $c$ anywhere.

steps: Take the diagram shape $J$ with objects $1$ and $2$ and no arrows.
A diagram of this shape is a pair of objects $A_1$ and $A_2$.
A colimit of it is an object $L$ with maps $A_1\to L$ and $A_2\to L$ that is universal, which is the coproduct $A_1\sqcup A_2$.
links.why: It shows that the coproduct is the colimit over a discrete diagram.

steps: Take the diagram shape $J$ with objects $1,2,3$ and arrows $2\to1$ and $2\to3$.
A diagram of this shape is a span $B\leftarrow A\to C$.
A colimit of it is a universal object $P$ with maps from $B$ and $C$ that agree on $A$, which is the pushout.
links.why: It shows that the pushout is the colimit over a span.

steps: Take the diagram shape $J$ to be a directed poset, so any two indices have a common upper bound.
A diagram of this shape is a system of objects $A_i$ with maps $A_i\to A_j$ for $i\le j$.
Its colimit is the directed colimit, which is the union when all maps are inclusions.
links.why: It shows that a directed colimit is the colimit over a directed index poset.

reminder: Points are collinear when one straight line contains all of them.
definition: Points $A_1,\dots,A_k$ are collinear if there is a single [line](c:line) that contains all of these [points](c:point). Three points $A,B,C$ of the plane are collinear exactly when the vectors $B-A$ and $C-A$ are linearly dependent, which means the determinant of their coordinates is $0$. Equivalently, three points are collinear when they are not [affinely independent](c:affine-independence).
examples: The points $(0,0)$, $(1,2)$ and $(2,4)$ lie on the line $y=2x$, so they are collinear.
Any two points are collinear, since a line passes through both.
In Pappus's hexagon theorem, the three intersection points of opposite sides of the hexagon are collinear.
Non-example: the vertices of a triangle are three points that lie on no common line.

reminder: A compact manifold is a manifold in which every open cover has a finite subcover.
definition: A compact manifold is a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ that is a [compact space](c:compact-space), so every cover of $M$ by open sets has a finite subcover. A compact manifold without boundary is often called closed.
examples: The circle $S^1$ and the sphere $S^n$ are compact manifolds.
The torus $T^2=S^1\times S^1$ is a compact manifold, and so is the real projective plane.
Non-example: $\mathbb R^n$ is a manifold but not compact, because the cover by balls $B(0,k)$ has no finite subcover.
Non-example: the open interval $(0,1)$ is a manifold but not compact, since the sets $(1/k,1)$ cover it with no finite subcover.

steps: Take a compact manifold $M$ and forget that it is compact.
The space $M$ is still locally Euclidean and Hausdorff, so it is a manifold.
Compactness is the added condition: every open cover has a finite subcover.
links.why: It shows that every theorem about manifolds holds for compact manifolds, which add finiteness arguments.

steps: Take a compact Riemann surface $X$.
Forget its complex structure; $X$ is a compact smooth manifold of real dimension $2$.
So a compact Riemann surface is a compact manifold with a complex structure added.
links.why: It shows that compact Riemann surfaces are compact surfaces with extra complex structure.

reminder: A compact Riemann surface is a connected complex manifold of dimension one that is compact.
definition: A compact Riemann surface is a [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface), that is a connected one-dimensional [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold), that is also a [compact space](c:compact-space). As a topological surface, it is a closed orientable surface of some genus $g\ge0$.
examples: The Riemann sphere $\mathbb{CP}^1=\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$ is a compact Riemann surface of genus $0$.
A complex torus $\mathbb C/\Lambda$ for a lattice $\Lambda$ is a compact Riemann surface of genus $1$.
The smooth projective curve $y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbb C$ is a compact Riemann surface of genus $1$.
Non-example: the complex plane $\mathbb C$ is a Riemann surface but not compact, and neither is the open unit disc.

steps: Take a compact Riemann surface $X$.
It is a connected one-dimensional complex manifold, so it is a Riemann surface.
Compactness is the added condition, and it makes $X$ a closed orientable surface of finite genus.
links.why: It shows that general Riemann surface theory applies to compact ones, which add finiteness.

reminder: A function has compact support if the closure of the set where it is nonzero is compact.
definition: Let $f\colon X\to V$ be a [function](c:function) from a [topological space](c:topological-space) to a [vector space](c:vector-space). The [support](c:support) of $f$ is the closure of $\{x:f(x)\neq0\}$, and $f$ has compact support if its support is a [compact subspace](c:compact-subspace) of $X$. On $\mathbb R^n$ this means that $f$ vanishes outside some bounded set.
examples: A [bump function](c:bump-function) on $\mathbb R$ that is $0$ outside $[-1,1]$ has compact support.
The indicator function of $[0,1]$ has compact support $[0,1]$, though it is not continuous.
Every function on a compact space has compact support, because closed subsets of compact spaces are compact.
Non-example: $e^{-x^2}$ is nonzero at every point of $\mathbb R$, so its support is $\mathbb R$, which is not compact.

reminder: The conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ is the probability of $A\cap B$ divided by the probability of $B$.
definition: For a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$ and events $A,B$ with $P(B)>0$, the conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ is $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$. It is the probability that $A$ occurs once one knows that $B$ occurs, and $P(\cdot\mid B)$ is again a probability measure. Events $A$ and $B$ are [independent](c:independence) exactly when $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$.
examples: For a fair die, $P(\text{six}\mid\text{even})=\frac{1/6}{1/2}=\frac13$.
Draw two cards without replacement; the probability that the second is an ace given that the first is an ace is $3/51$.
Bayes' rule follows from the definition: $P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)\,P(A)/P(B)$.
Non-example: $P(A\mid B)$ is not $P(B\mid A)$; for a fair die, $P(\text{even}\mid\text{six})=1$ but $P(\text{six}\mid\text{even})=\frac13$.

steps: Take an event $A$ and its indicator function $1_A$.
The average of $1_A$ over the event $B$ is $P(A\cap B)/P(B)$.
That average is $P(A\mid B)$, so conditional probability is the conditional expectation of an indicator.
links.why: It shows that conditional probability is the special case of conditional expectation for indicator functions.

reminder: A division ring is a ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
definition: A division ring is a [ring](c:ring) $D$ with $1\neq0$ in which every nonzero element $a$ has an element $b$ with $ab=ba=1$. Its multiplication need not be commutative.
examples: Every [field](c:field), such as $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, is a division ring.
The [quaternions](c:quaternion) $\mathbb H$ form a division ring that is not commutative, because $ij=-ji$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z$ is a ring, but $2$ has no inverse in $\mathbb Z$, so it is not a division ring.
Non-example: the ring of $2\times2$ real matrices has nonzero elements without inverses, such as $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$.

steps: Take a field $F$, which has commutative multiplication and an inverse for every nonzero element.
So $F$ is a ring in which every nonzero element has an inverse, that is, a division ring.
A division ring is a field exactly when its multiplication is commutative.
links.why: It shows that fields are the commutative division rings.

steps: Take a division ring $D$ and keep its addition and multiplication.
These satisfy the ring axioms, so $D$ is a ring.
The added condition is $1\neq0$ and an inverse for every nonzero element.
links.why: It shows that ring theory applies to division rings, which add inverses.

reminder: The exponential map sends a tangent vector to the point reached after time one along its geodesic or one-parameter subgroup.
definition: On a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold), the exponential map at $p$ sends a vector $v$ of the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) $T_pM$ to $\gamma_v(1)$, where $\gamma_v$ is the [geodesic](c:geodesic) with $\gamma_v(0)=p$ and $\gamma_v'(0)=v$. On a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ it sends $X$ in the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) to $\gamma(1)$, where $\gamma$ is the one-parameter subgroup with $\gamma'(0)=X$.
examples: On the unit sphere, $\exp_p(v)$ moves a distance $|v|$ along the great circle that starts in the direction $v$.
For $G=GL_n(\mathbb R)$, the exponential map is the matrix exponential $\exp(A)=\sum_{k\ge0}A^k/k!$.
On $\mathbb R^n$ with the flat metric, $\exp_p(v)=p+v$.
Non-example: on the open unit disc with the flat metric, $\exp_0(v)$ is not defined for $|v|\ge1$, because the geodesic leaves the disc before time one.

steps: Take the Lie group $G=(\mathbb R_{>0},\cdot)$ with Lie algebra $\mathbb R$.
The one-parameter subgroup with initial velocity $x$ is $t\mapsto e^{tx}$.
So the exponential map of $G$ sends $x$ to $e^x$.
links.why: It shows that the exponential map generalizes the real exponential function to groups and manifolds.

reminder: A field extension $L/K$ is a field $L$ that contains the field $K$ as a subfield.
definition: A field extension, written $L/K$, is a pair of [fields](c:field) $K\subseteq L$ in which the operations of $K$ are the restrictions of those of $L$. Then $L$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) over $K$, and its dimension $[L:K]$ is the degree of the extension.
examples: The extension $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ has degree $2$, with the basis $1,i$.
The extension $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$ has degree $2$, with the basis $1,\sqrt2$.
The extension $\mathbb R/\mathbb Q$ has infinite degree.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Q$ is an inclusion of rings, but $\mathbb Z$ is not a field, so $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is not a field extension.

steps: Take an algebraic extension $L/K$, in which every element of $L$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial over $K$.
Ignore that condition; $K\subseteq L$ is still a pair of fields.
So $L/K$ is a field extension, and being algebraic is an extra condition.
links.why: It shows that algebraic extensions are the field extensions whose elements are all algebraic.

steps: Take a number field $L$, a field that contains $\mathbb Q$ and has finite degree over $\mathbb Q$.
Then $\mathbb Q\subseteq L$ is a pair of fields.
So $L/\mathbb Q$ is a field extension, with base field $\mathbb Q$ and finite degree as the added conditions.
links.why: It shows that number fields are the finite field extensions of the rational numbers.

reminder: A Fourier series expands a periodic function into a sum of sines and cosines.
definition: For a [periodic function](c:periodic-function) $f$ of period $2\pi$ that is integrable on $[0,2\pi]$, the Fourier series is $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_ne^{inx}$ with $c_n=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-inx}\,dx$. It is a [trigonometric series](c:trigonometric-series) in the [exponential functions](c:exponential-function) $e^{inx}$, or in sines and cosines, whose coefficients are [integrals](c:integral) of $f$ against these functions.
examples: The function $\cos3x$ is its own Fourier series, with $c_3=c_{-3}=\tfrac12$ and all other $c_n=0$.
The square wave that equals $1$ on $(0,\pi)$ and $-1$ on $(-\pi,0)$ has the series $\frac4\pi\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\sin(2k+1)x}{2k+1}$.
The sawtooth $f(x)=x$ on $(-\pi,\pi)$ has the series $2\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{\sin nx}{n}$.
Non-example: $\sum_{n\ge1}\sin nx$ is not the Fourier series of any integrable function, because its coefficients do not tend to $0$.

steps: Take the Fourier series $\sum c_ne^{inx}$ of an integrable function $f$.
Write $e^{inx}=\cos nx+i\sin nx$ to turn it into a trigonometric series.
The added condition is that each coefficient $c_n$ is the integral $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-inx}\,dx$.
links.why: It shows that a Fourier series is a trigonometric series whose coefficients come from one function.

reminder: A Galois extension is an algebraic field extension in which the automorphisms over the base field fix exactly the base field.
definition: A [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$ is Galois if it is an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) that is normal and separable. Equivalently, the fixed field of its [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) $\mathrm{Aut}(L/K)$ is exactly $K$.
examples: The extension $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$ is Galois, with the automorphisms $\sqrt2\mapsto\pm\sqrt2$.
The extension $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is Galois, with the automorphisms identity and complex conjugation.
The splitting field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2,\omega)$ of $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb Q$, with $\omega$ a primitive cube root of unity, is Galois with a group of order $6$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)/\mathbb Q$ is not Galois, because its only automorphism is the identity and the fixed field is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$, not $\mathbb Q$.

steps: Take a Galois extension $L/K$.
By definition it is algebraic, so it is an algebraic extension.
Normality and separability are added: each irreducible polynomial over $K$ with a root in $L$ splits in $L$ with distinct roots.
links.why: It shows that Galois extensions are the algebraic extensions with enough automorphisms.

reminder: The Galois group of a field extension is the group of automorphisms of the larger field that fix the smaller field.
definition: For a [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$, the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ is the [group](c:group) of all field automorphisms $\sigma$ of $L$ with $\sigma(a)=a$ for every $a\in K$, with composition as the product. It is a subgroup of the [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) of $L$.
examples: The group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb C/\mathbb R)$ has two elements, the identity and complex conjugation.
The group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/\mathbb Q)$ is $\mathbb Z/2\times\mathbb Z/2$.
The group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb F_{p^n}/\mathbb F_p)$ is cyclic of order $n$, generated by the Frobenius map $x\mapsto x^p$.
Non-example: complex conjugation is not in $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb C/\mathbb Q(i))$, because it sends $i$ to $-i$ and so does not fix the base field.

steps: Take the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$ of the field $L$.
Keep only the automorphisms that fix every element of $K$.
These form a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$, the Galois group, and fixing $K$ is the added condition.
links.why: It shows that the Galois group is the part of the automorphism group that respects the base field.

reminder: A Gaussian measure is a probability measure whose image under every continuous linear functional is a normal distribution.
definition: A [Borel](c:borel-measure) [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\gamma$ on $\mathbb R^n$, or on a [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) $E$, is Gaussian if for every continuous linear functional $\ell$ the image measure $\gamma\circ\ell^{-1}$ on $\mathbb R$ is a [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution). A point mass counts as a degenerate normal distribution with variance $0$.
examples: The standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$ has the density $(2\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/2}$.
A point mass $\delta_a$ is a degenerate Gaussian measure, because every linear image is a point mass.
Wiener measure on the space $C[0,1]$ of continuous paths is a Gaussian measure.
Non-example: the uniform distribution on $[0,1]$ is not Gaussian, because its image under the identity functional is not normal.

steps: Take a normal distribution $N(m,\sigma^2)$ on $\mathbb R$.
Its image under every linear map $x\mapsto cx$ is again normal, with mean $cm$ and variance $c^2\sigma^2$.
So it is a Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R$, the one-dimensional case.
links.why: It shows that Gaussian measures extend the normal distribution to higher dimensions and infinite-dimensional spaces.

reminder: Random variables are iid when they are independent and all have the same distribution.
definition: A family $X_1,X_2,\dots$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) is iid, that is independent and identically distributed, if the variables are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and every $X_i$ has the same law, so $P(X_i\in B)=P(X_1\in B)$ for all measurable $B$. Equivalently, the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of $X_1,\dots,X_n$ is the product of $n$ copies of one distribution.
examples: The results of repeated tosses of one fair coin are iid.
Draws with replacement from one urn are iid.
The sample $X_1,\dots,X_n$ in the law of large numbers is assumed iid.
Non-example: draws without replacement from a finite urn have the same distribution but are not independent.

steps: Take iid random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$.
By definition they are independent, so they form a family of independent random variables.
Identical distribution is the added condition: all marginal laws agree.
links.why: It shows that every result for independent variables applies to iid variables, which add one shared law.

reminder: A line bundle is a vector bundle whose fibres are all one-dimensional.
definition: A line bundle over a space $X$ is a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $L\to X$ of rank one: each fibre $L_x$ is a one-dimensional [vector space](c:vector-space), and over small open sets $U\subseteq X$ the bundle is isomorphic to $U\times\mathbb K$.
examples: The trivial bundle $X\times\mathbb R$ is a line bundle over any space $X$.
The Moebius strip is a nontrivial real line bundle over the circle.
The tautological bundle over projective space has, as its fibre over a line $\ell$, the line $\ell$ itself.
Non-example: the tangent bundle of the $2$-sphere has rank $2$, so it is not a line bundle.

steps: Take a line bundle $L\to X$.
Each fibre is a vector space and $L$ is locally trivial, so $L$ is a vector bundle.
Rank one is the added condition: every fibre has dimension one.
links.why: It shows that vector bundle constructions, such as duals and tensor products, apply to line bundles.

steps: Take a complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$.
Form the top exterior power $\wedge^nT^*X$ of its cotangent bundle.
Its fibres are one-dimensional, so it is a line bundle over $X$.
links.why: It shows that the canonical bundle is a line bundle built from the manifold itself.

reminder: A measure space is a set with a sigma-algebra of measurable subsets and a measure on it.
definition: A measure space is a triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ of a [set](c:set) $X$, a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal A$ of subsets of $X$, and a [measure](c:measure) $\mu\colon\mathcal A\to[0,\infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ that is countably additive on disjoint sets.
examples: The real line with the Borel sets and [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) is a measure space.
The natural numbers with all subsets and counting measure form a measure space.
Every probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a measure space with $P(\Omega)=1$.

Non-example: the triple $(\mathbb R,\mathcal P(\mathbb R),\lambda)$ is not a measure space for a translation-invariant $\lambda$ with $\lambda([0,1])=1$, because a Vitali set shows that no such $\lambda$ exists.

reminder: The midpoint of a segment is the point of the segment that is equally far from both ends.
definition: The midpoint of a [line segment](c:line-segment) $AB$ is the [point](c:point) $M$ of the segment with $|AM|=|MB|$ in [distance](c:distance). In coordinates, $M=(A+B)/2$.
examples: The midpoint of $(0,0)$ and $(4,2)$ is $(2,1)$.
On the number line, the midpoint of $a$ and $b$ is $(a+b)/2$.
In a triangle, the midpoints of the three sides are the vertices of the medial triangle.
Non-example: for $A=(0,0)$ and $B=(4,0)$, the point $(2,5)$ is equally far from both but is not on the segment, so it is not the midpoint.

reminder: A monad is an endofunctor with a unit and a multiplication that obey unit and associativity laws.
definition: A monad on a [category](c:category) $C$ is an [endofunctor](c:endofunctor) $T\colon C\to C$ with [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation) $\eta\colon 1_C\to T$ (the unit) and $\mu\colon T^2\to T$ (the multiplication) such that $\mu\circ T\mu=\mu\circ\mu T$ and $\mu\circ T\eta=\mu\circ\eta T=1_T$.
examples: The list monad on sets sends $X$ to the finite lists in $X$; $\eta$ makes one-element lists and $\mu$ concatenates a list of lists.
The power-set monad on sets has $\eta(x)=\{x\}$ and $\mu$ the union of a set of sets.
The functor $T(X)=M\times X$ for a monoid $M$ is a monad, with the monoid laws as the monad laws.
Non-example: the endofunctor $T(X)=\varnothing$ on sets has no unit $X\to T(X)$ when $X$ is not empty, so it is not a monad.

steps: Take a monoid $M$ with unit $e$ and product $m$.
Define $T(X)=M\times X$ on sets with $\eta(x)=(e,x)$ and $\mu(a,(b,x))=(m(a,b),x)$.
The monoid laws are exactly the unit and associativity laws of a monad, so $T$ is a monad.
links.why: It shows that every monoid gives a monad, and that a monad is a monoid-like structure on endofunctors.

reminder: The order of a group element $g$ is the least positive integer $n$ with $g^n=e$.
definition: For an element $g$ of a [group](c:group) with [identity element](c:identity-element) $e$, the order of $g$ is the least positive [integer](c:natural-number) $n$ with $g^n=e$, or infinity if there is none. It equals the number of elements of the [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $\langle g\rangle$ generated by $g$.
examples: In $\mathbb Z/6$, the element $2$ has order $3$, because $2+2+2=0$.
A transposition in the symmetric group $S_n$ has order $2$.
In $(\mathbb Z,+)$, the element $1$ has infinite order, because no positive multiple of $1$ is $0$.
Non-example: the order of an element is not the number of elements of the group; in $\mathbb Z/6$ the element $2$ has order $3$, not $6$.

reminder: A principal $G$-bundle is a fibre bundle with a group action that is free and transitive on each fibre.
definition: For a [Lie group](c:lie-group) or topological group $G$, a principal $G$-bundle is a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) $\pi\colon P\to X$ with a continuous right [action](c:group-action) of $G$ on $P$ that preserves each fibre and is free and transitive on it. Over small open sets $U\subseteq X$, the bundle is isomorphic to $U\times G$ with $G$ acting by right multiplication.
examples: The Hopf fibration $S^3\to S^2$ is a principal $U(1)$-bundle.
The frame bundle of an $n$-dimensional manifold is a principal $GL_n(\mathbb R)$-bundle.
The trivial bundle $X\times G\to X$ is a principal $G$-bundle.
Non-example: the bundle $\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ has fibre $[0,1]$, and no group acts transitively on $[0,1]$ by homeomorphisms, because the endpoints differ from interior points.

steps: Take a principal $G$-bundle $P\to X$.
It is locally trivial with fibre $G$, so it is a fibre bundle.
The added structure is a free and transitive action of $G$ on each fibre.
links.why: It shows that every fibre bundle result applies to principal bundles, which carry a group action.

reminder: A projective module is a direct summand of a free module.
definition: An $R$-[module](c:module) $P$ is projective if it is a direct summand of a [free module](c:free-module), that is, $P\oplus Q\cong F$ for some module $Q$ and some free module $F$, using the [direct sum](c:direct-sum). Equivalently, every surjection $M\to P$ of $R$-modules has a section $P\to M$.
examples: Every free module, such as $R^n$, is projective.
Over $\mathbb Z/6$, the module $\mathbb Z/3$ is projective but not free, because $\mathbb Z/6\cong\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/3$.
Every module over a field is projective, because every vector space is free.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z/2$ is not projective over $\mathbb Z$, because the surjection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2$ has no section, as $\mathbb Z$ has no element of order $2$.

steps: Take a free module $F$ over $R$.
It is a direct summand of itself, with complement $0$.
So $F$ is projective; projective modules are the direct summands of free modules, and they need not be free.
links.why: It shows that free modules are projective, and that projectivity is the weaker, more flexible condition.

reminder: The elements of the quotient group $G/N$ are the cosets of the normal subgroup $N$, multiplied by $(aN)(bN)=abN$.
definition: For a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) $N$ of a [group](c:group) $G$, the quotient group $G/N$ is the set of [cosets](c:coset) $aN$ with the product $(aN)(bN)=abN$. This product is well defined exactly because $N$ is normal, and $a\mapsto aN$ is a surjective [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $G\to G/N$ with kernel $N$.
examples: The integers modulo $n$ form the quotient group $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$.
The quotient $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is the circle group.
The quotient $S_n/A_n$ has two elements and is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z/2$.
Non-example: for $H=\{e,(1\,2)\}$ in $S_3$, which is not normal, the rule $(aH)(bH)=abH$ depends on the chosen representatives, so the cosets do not form a group this way.

reminder: A set-valued functor is representable when it is naturally isomorphic to a hom-functor.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F\colon C\to\mathbf{Set}$ is representable if there are an object $X$ of $C$ and a [natural isomorphism](c:natural-isomorphism) $F\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)$ with the [hom-functor](c:hom-functor); a [contravariant functor](c:contravariant-functor) $F$ is representable if $F\cong\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)$. The object $X$ is unique up to unique isomorphism, and the isomorphism corresponds to one universal element of $F(X)$.
examples: The forgetful functor $\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is represented by the group $\mathbb Z$, because $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb Z,G)\cong G$.
The forgetful functor $\mathbf{Vect}_K\to\mathbf{Set}$ is represented by the vector space $K$.
The contravariant functor $X\mapsto\{\text{open subsets of }X\}$ on spaces is represented by the Sierpinski space $\mathbb S$, because open sets of $X$ correspond to continuous maps $X\to\mathbb S$.

Non-example: the covariant power-set functor $\mathbf{Set}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is not representable, because $P(1\times1)$ has $2$ elements but $P(1)\times P(1)$ has $4$, and representable functors preserve products.

steps: Take a hom-functor $\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)$.
It is naturally isomorphic to itself by the identity, so it is representable.
A representable functor is any functor naturally isomorphic to some hom-functor.
links.why: It shows that representable functors are the functors that look like a hom-functor up to natural isomorphism.

reminder: An $n$th root of unity in a ring is an element $x$ with $x^n=1$.
definition: In a [ring](c:ring) $R$, an $n$th root of unity is an element $x$ with $x^n=1$, that is, a [root](c:root) of the [equation](c:equation) $x^n-1=0$. In $\mathbb C$ the $n$th roots of unity are the numbers $e^{2\pi ik/n}$ for $k=0,\dots,n-1$.
examples: In $\mathbb C$, the fourth roots of unity are $1$, $i$, $-1$ and $-i$.
In $\mathbb Z/7$, the element $2$ is a third root of unity, because $2^3=8\equiv1$.
In $\mathbb R$, the only roots of unity are $1$ and $-1$.
Non-example: $2$ is not a root of unity in $\mathbb R$, because $2^n=1$ has no solution with $n\ge1$.

steps: Take an element $x$ of a ring with $x^n=1$.
Then $x$ is a root of the polynomial $p(t)=t^n-1$.
So roots of unity are the roots of the special polynomials $t^n-1$.
links.why: It shows that roots of unity are roots of one family of polynomials, so root results apply.

reminder: The shadow of a family of $k$-element sets is the family of all $(k-1)$-element subsets of its members.
definition: For a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) $\mathcal F$ in which every set has $k$ elements, the shadow $\partial\mathcal F$ is the family of all $(k-1)$-element [subsets](c:subset) of members of $\mathcal F$. Equivalently, $\partial\mathcal F=\{F\setminus\{x\}:F\in\mathcal F,\ x\in F\}$, for sets from a [finite set](c:finite-set).
examples: The shadow of a single $k$-element set has exactly $k$ members.
The shadow of all $k$-subsets of an $n$-set is the family of all $(k-1)$-subsets of that $n$-set.
Non-example: the family of $(k+1)$-sets that contain a member of $\mathcal F$ is the upper shadow, not the shadow.
